full_judgment:
There was a contract in 1986 between the plaintiff and the defendants for construction of a fuel storage tank at Jessore Cantonment under contract No.DW and CE (AIR) 01/86 dated 8-3-1986 and accordingly, work order was given for the said work at a cost of Taka 7,37,107.30. The work was supposed to be completed within 7-7-1986 as the tender for the respondent was accepted for construction of the said work. The defendant apprehended that the balance work might not be completed within the stipulated period of time and as such, its contract was cancelled. By appointing a new contractor the balance work was completed. The plaintiff then filed an application under section 8(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 for appointment of an arbitrator in Miscellaneous Case No.360 of 1989. Before filing of such application he requested the appellants for appointment of an arbitrator but to no avail. The Court then appointed Chief Engineer of MES as the sole arbitrator to hear and publish award. After hearing, the sole arbitrator passed an award and directed the appellants to pay a sum of Taka 9,99,900 on 5-9-1993 to the respondent. The appellant therefore filed an application under section 17 read with section 14 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 before the Court to make the award Rule of the Court in Title Suit No.36 of 2001. 

 II. The facts and circumstances of the decision relied on being distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the present case, the High Court Division erred in law in allowing the appeal. 

 10. The appellants and the respondent entered into a contract on 15-2-1986 for construction of a fuel storage tank at Jessore Cantonment. Pursuant to the contract No.DW and CE (AIR) 01/86 dated 8-3-1986 between the parties work order was issued to the defendant. The estimated cost of aforesaid work was fixed at Taka 7,37,107.30 and the work was to be completed within 7-7-1986. After lapse of sometime, the appellants apprehended that the balance work might not be completed within the stipulated period of time and as such, final notice for cancellation of the contract was issued on 26-5-1986. The appellants appointed a new contractor and completed the balance work. By filing an application under section 8(2) of the Arbitration Act, the respondent prayed for appointment of an arbitrator and as such, Miscellaneous Case No.360 of 1989 was initiated. The Court appointed the Chief Engineer of MES as the sole-arbitrator to hear and publish the award. The sole arbitrator passed an award of Taka 9,99,900 on 5-9-1993 and directed the appellants to pay the amount to the claimant. 

 11. On perusal of the award, the trial Court found that while preparing the award the Arbitrator did not assign the reason for passing the award in favour of the respondent. The arbitrator even did not take into notice that the contract entered into between the parties was cancelled. The trial Court noticed that the arbitrator did not state why the appellants were liable to pay the amount mentioned in the award. The respondent contended that the appellants neither deposited the amount mentioned in the award nor furnished any security therefor as requirement for contesting the miscellaneous case for arbitration. The trial Court also found that the arbitrator did not consider the dispute between the parties before passing an award and as such, the aforesaid acts of the arbitrator amount to misconduct. 

 12. The High Court Division came to a finding that the appellants contested the suit but they neither deposited the amount of the award nor furnished any security to the satisfaction of the Court in order to comply with section 33 of the Arbitration Act. The High Court Division with reference to the case of Bangladesh vs KM Shafi Ltd, 43 DLR (AD) 217 came to a finding that the decision of the arbitrator is not a judgment and it need not contain the reasoning’s of the arbitrator. The High Court Division held that the trial Court found fault with the decision made by the arbitrator and dismissed the suit and therefore, the judgment delivered by the trial Court was required to be set-aside according to the case cited above. The High Court Division came to a finding that in the case in hand one of the parties went to the Court to make the award Rule of the Court and that required no evidence. Therefore, the High Court Division allowed the appeal and affirmed the award passed by the Arbitrator and directed the appellants to pay interest at the rate of 16% to the respondent till realization of the amount mentioned in the award. 

 13. Admittedly, the parties entered into a contract on 15-5-1986 for construction of a fuel storage tank at Jessore Cantonment under a contract No.DW & CE (AIR)01/86 dated 8-3-1986. In the aforesaid contract the cost of construction work was assessed to Taka 7,37,107.30 and that the work was to be completed within 3 (three) months i.e. before 7-6-1986 which was a condition precedent. The general conditions of the contract have been filed by the appellants in the additional paper book dated 12-9-2019. Clauses 53(c) and (d) stipulated the grounds of cancellation of the contract for default. Clause 61 of the aforesaid contract states, amongst others, that if the contractor's representative fails to attend when required, the Engineer-in-Charge shall have power to proceed by himself to take measurements and in that case these measurements shall be accepted by the contractor as final. 

 19. It is necessary to remember here that clause-61 of the contract, amongst others, states that if the contractor's representative fails to attend when required, the Engineer-in-charge shall have power to proceed by himself to take measurements and in that case these measurements shall be accepted by the contractor as final. 

 20. In the case in hand, the contractor was notified to be present for joint measurements to be held on 10-7-1986 but the representative of the respondent refrained to attend when the joint measurements was taken. Therefore, he is bound to accept the measurements made by a four-member-committee. The four-member-committee found that the amount of money spent on the date of joint measurements was Taka 67,831.30. Therefore, the respondent could claim only the aforesaid amount and not more. The letter dated 26-5-1986 reveals that the respondent was paid the running bill although he did not deposit the earnest money till that date. 

 21. What is surprising to note here is that the estimated cost for completion of the work was assessed to Taka 7,37,107.30 but the arbitrator passed an award for Taka 9,99,900. The contractor (respondent) submitted a claim for more than Taka 20,00,000 (twenty lac). Having gone through the award, we find that the arbitrator has not assigned any reason for passing award in each of the items. The contractor claimed more than Taka 20,00,000 (twenty lac) in eight items. The award reveals that the arbitrator without looking for supporting evidence and without considering any material for being satisfied passed the award. Even the arbitrator did not rely on any documentary evidence while passing an award of Taka 9,99,900. This award passed by the arbitrator without assessment of actual cost incurred by the respondent-contractor is not only illegal but also without jurisdiction. By doing so, the arbitrator has committed misconduct. 

 22. The High Court Division found that as the appellants neither deposited the amount of award nor furnished the security as provided under section 33 of the Arbitration Act, they were debarred from challenging the award passed by the arbitrator. While making the aforesaid finding, the High Court Division relied upon the decision made in the case of Bangladesh vs KM Shafi Ltd., 43 DLR (AD) 21 (ibid). We have gone through the decision and found that the High Court Division only relied upon two sentences of the aforesaid reported case. If the aforesaid case was considered in full, the High Court Division would have found that the decision of the Appellate Division was otherwise. Paragraph 8 of the aforesaid reported case, reveals that the arbitrator (Superintending Engineer) asked the Executive Engineer, Roads and Highway Department, Dhaka to examine the bills and papers and by memo Nos.605 dated 4-4-1988 and 781 dated 19-4-1988, the Executive Engineer "as per direction of the highest Court", examining the contractor's bills and verifying the quantum of work done and the rates, submitted reports. In the cited case considering the Contractor's bills and papers and those reports, the contractor's dues came to Taka 5,59,680.02. Therefore, from the cited case, it appears that the arbitrator applied his mind while passing the award. Therefore, the findings of the cited case that there is indeed no particular form for expression of arbitrator's decision and that it is not a judgment and it need not contain the reasoning’s of the arbitrator. In view of the discussion made above, there is no scope for reading two lines of the aforesaid reported decision in isolation. 

 23. In the case in hand, the Arbitrator was under the obligation to consider the actual work done by the contractor in view of the positive case of the appellants that the contractor only completed 10% of the work. The award does not reflect that the arbitrator considered any voucher while passing award in each of the items mentioned in the disputed award. Therefore, the aforesaid reported case has manner of application to the case in hand and rather the reported case goes against the respondent. 

 25. In this connection, reliance may be placed on the case of Project Director PL and another vs A Latif Company Ltd, 19 BLC (AD) 199 where it has been held in paragraph-18 as under: 

 26. From the above cited case, it appears that if the award is otherwise patently illegal or void, it would be open to the Court to consider the defect in the award suo motu and when the Courts act suo motu, the question of limitation does not arise. Moreover, when the Court acts suo motu not no question regarding making of deposit can arise. Therefore, we are of the view that though the appellants did not comply with the provision of section 33 of the Arbitration Act, the trial Court was perfectly justified in not passing an award because the award was patently illegal and void. 

 27. Having considered the materials on record, the trial Court held that by passing the award the arbitrator committed misconduct. 

 28. The action of the arbitrator amounts to misconduct when arbitrator ignores material documents produced and no award can be given without any basis and an arbitrator must look into all the papers and documents produced before it prior to making an award (KP Poulose vs State of Kerala, AIR 1975 SC 1259. 

 29. In the case of Union of India is M/s Mahta Teja Singh & Co, AIR 1983 Delhi 297, it has been held that the conduct of the arbitrator in making the award allowing the claim without himself looking into the report on which the claim was based and without allowing the respondent an opportunity of inspection thereof, amounts to misconduct of the arbitration proceedings, resulting denial of natural justice and thus rendered the award liable to be set-aside. 

 30. Misconduct is not a connotation of moral lapse. It comprises legal misconduct which is complete if the Arbitrator on the face of the award arrives at an inconsistent conclusion even on his own finding or arrives at a decision by ignoring very material documents, which throw abundant light on the controversy to arrive at a just and fair decision and it is in this sense that arbitrator has misconducted the proceeding in the case. In this case there can be no hesitation in setting aside such award. 

 33. The High Court Division came to the finding that in this case one of the parties went to make the award Rule of the Court and that required no evidence.
